name: Tongue tie release

card.summary: Frenotomy releases the tissue under the tongue; it has feeding evidence in infants, but claims about facial symmetry are untested.
card.note: Evidence concerns feeding and speech; no study tests it for facial appearance.

quick.overview:
Tongue-tie release cuts the frenulum under the tongue to improve tongue mobility. It is mostly used for infant breastfeeding problems, and sometimes for speech or mobility in older patients.
Online, some people link it to palate shape, jaw development and facial symmetry. These links are described as hypothesised, and no study was found testing release for appearance.
quick.mechanism: A short incision or removal of the frenulum, using scissors, a scalpel or a laser, frees the tongue. Proponents of the symmetry idea say better tongue posture could influence the palate and jaw; this is described as speculative.
quick.risks: The procedure is typically quick with little reported pain. Experts debate overdiagnosis of minor restrictions, and reviews describe long-term benefits for feeding duration and speech as inconclusive.

lead: Tongue-tie release, also called frenotomy or frenectomy, is a minor procedure that cuts or removes the lingual frenulum, the fold of tissue anchoring the tongue to the floor of the mouth, in people with ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) [1][2]. It can be done with scissors, a scalpel or a laser, and a related procedure, frenuloplasty, adds suturing for more complex cases [1][2]. Its established use is to free tongue movement for infant feeding and, in some children and adults, for speech or mobility [2][12].

In looksmaxxing and related online discussion, release is raised as a way to let the tongue rest against the palate, which people connect with palate shape, jaw development, facial symmetry and a better side profile. The chain they describe runs from a freer tongue to better resting tongue posture to a broader palate and more forward jaw growth; a looksmax.org poster in his mid-twenties asked whether release would help his side profile, and a reply said that relapse after surgery was possible if the tongue could not be held up [22]. Wikipedia describes the links between tongue-tie and a narrow palate, crowding or an open bite as proposed associations, not established outcomes [2].

Research on the procedure itself is substantial for feeding. A 2017 Cochrane review of five randomized trials found that frenotomy reduced maternal nipple pain in the short term but did not consistently improve infant breastfeeding [9], while a 2024 meta-analysis of 21 studies reported improved breastfeeding self-efficacy and reduced nipple pain after frenotomy [10]. A 2024 meta-analysis of ten speech studies associated frenectomy with improved articulation in selected children [11]. No study found tests release as a way to change facial symmetry or appearance.
infobox: Estimated 4 to 11% of newborns in the Cochrane review; 5-8% in other estimates, varying with criteria [1][9]
Often none or local, with quick recovery reported [2]

chain: Frenulum is released and the tongue can lift
Tongue rests more easily against the palate (proposed)
angle.text: Release frees the tongue so it can reach the roof of the mouth. People interested in facial structure link that tongue posture to palate and jaw development and to a better profile, while the documented uses are feeding, speech and mobility.

paras: A frenectomy is the removal or incision of a frenulum. The main variants are lingual frenectomy, which releases the tongue attachment, and labial frenectomy, which treats lip attachments associated with gingival recession or a gap between the front teeth [1][20]. Frenotomy usually means a simple incision, often in infants, while frenuloplasty implies a reconstructive revision with sutures [1]. Wikipedia lists further types of frenectomy at other sites, including interdental and genital [20].

Ankyloglossia is a congenital condition in which a short or thick lingual frenulum restricts tongue-tip movement. Severity ranges from a thin mucous band to full tethering of the tongue to the floor of the mouth [2]. As of 2025, Wikipedia states that no definition, classification or diagnostic criteria has been generally accepted; the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine recommends a severity scale grading appearance and function, and Hazelbaker's 1993 tool is one such assessment [2]. A 2017 JAMA Otolaryngology review called for consistent terminology emphasising symptomatic ankyloglossia and a uniform grading system such as the Hazelbaker tool or Coryllos grading [12]. The cause is unknown, though it may be heritable and is associated with rare syndromes [2].

The Cochrane review states that tongue-tie is present in 4% to 11% of newborns, and meta-analyses elsewhere estimate about 5% to 8%, with rates varying with the diagnostic method and higher in newborns presenting with breastfeeding difficulty [9][1]. Professionals disagree on how often it causes problems: some consider it rarely symptomatic and others link it to many issues [2]. A 2009 review in the Journal of Periodontology examined facts and myths in diagnosis and treatment [3].

The 2017 JAMA Otolaryngology review described wide variation in medical practice and a lack of high-quality clinical studies, noted that frenotomy is a low-risk procedure that is likely to be beneficial with careful patient selection, and said the natural history of untreated ankyloglossia is not well documented [12]. Wikipedia reports that in 2020 professionals raised concern about a rise in unnecessary infant frenectomies, partly driven by online parenting groups, and that public healthcare such as the NHS may not cover the procedure while private clinics remain available [20]. A 2022 systematic review on the upper lip reported a 10-fold increase in frenectomies since 2000 and suggested parents' exposure to online advice about breastfeeding and aesthetics may encourage requests [14].

The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery published a Delphi consensus statement in 2020 by an expert panel of pediatric otolaryngologists: of 89 statements, 41 reached consensus, 17 were near consensus and 28 did not, covering topics such as ankyloglossia and sleep apnea, breastfeeding, frenotomy indications and informed consent, ankyloglossia in older children and the upper lip frenulum. The authors state that lack of consensus on other statements likely reflects knowledge gaps and lack of evidence [13].

Treatment is by frenotomy, a quick snip or laser release, or frenuloplasty, which also repairs the site, usually closed with dissolvable stitches; it is often done under local anaesthesia and most patients are reported to have little pain afterward [2]. Wikipedia describes the laser as offering predictable tissue response, fast ablation and immediate haemostasis [20]. A review of frenectomy surgical techniques covers lingual and labial procedures [24].

Randomised and comparative studies have looked at the techniques. A 2006 comparison of carbon dioxide laser and scalpel frenectomy assessed patient perceptions [5], a comparison of diode laser and Er:YAG laser in ankyloglossia was published in 2010 [6], and trials registered at ClinicalTrials.gov include frenotomy and frenectomy techniques for a high frenum attachment in adults (NCT06331325, n=46) and tongue mobility after frenectomy (NCT06856564, n=60) [7][8].

Non-surgical options include exercises from orofacial myology specialists, compensatory speech strategies and watchful waiting, since the frenulum is reported to recede between about six months and six years of age [2]. Adult release is discussed less in the literature; the NCT06331325 trial enrolled adults with a high frenum attachment [7].

A 2000 study by Messner and colleagues found breastfeeding difficulty in 25% of mothers of affected infants compared with 3% of controls, and a small series of ten infants reported immediate improvement for four after division [2]. A prospective cohort of tongue-tie and lip-tie release reported breastfeeding improvement afterward [4].

The Cochrane review of frenotomy in newborns included five randomized trials with 302 newborns. Pooled data from two studies of 155 infants showed no change on a 10-point feeding scale, one study of 58 infants found objective improvement on a 12-point scale, and three pooled studies of 212 mothers showed reduced nipple pain; no adverse effects were reported, but the authors noted serious methodological weaknesses, including small samples, limited blinding and control infants often receiving frenotomy anyway [9].

A 2014 randomised trial of 107 term infants under two weeks old with mild or moderate tongue-tie compared immediate frenotomy with standard breastfeeding support; at 5 days there was no difference in the primary breastfeeding outcome, but maternal self-efficacy was higher with frenotomy, and by 8 weeks only 6 of the 44 standard-care mothers who then requested frenotomy were breastfeeding without it [18]. A 2022 trial of 47 infants with posterior tongue-tie reported improvement on 11 objective feeding measures ten days after frenotomy, along with better self-efficacy and less nipple pain [17]. A double-blind sham-controlled trial of 112 newborn-mother pairs at Tampa General Hospital found no significant difference in LATCH or pain scores immediately after the procedure [15].

The UK FROSTTIE trial randomised 169 infants of a planned 870 before stopping early; breastmilk feeding at 3 months was 88% in the frenotomy arm and 86% in the support-only arm, and the authors said the trial could not determine whether frenotomy adds benefit [16]. The 2024 meta-analysis of 21 studies reported medium to large improvements in breastfeeding self-efficacy and nipple pain and a medium effect on infant reflux severity after frenotomy [10]. A 2023 literature review also addresses ankyloglossia as a barrier to breastfeeding [23].

sections.h: Research on speech, sleep and function
paras: For speech, a 2002 series of 30 children reported articulation improvement in nine of 15 evaluated after frenuloplasty, whereas several later systematic reviews and trials reported that ankyloglossia does not affect speech sound development [2]. The 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of ten studies, with an average patient age of 4.1 years, associated frenectomy with improved articulation (0.78, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.87), and concluded that it is suitable for select patients if caught early in childhood, while noting limited research [11].

A prospective cohort of 37 children (mean age 4.2 years) who had CO2 laser lingual frenectomy paired with myofunctional exercises reported improved speech, solid feeding and sleep on questionnaires at one week and one month, with improved speech in 89% [19]. Adults surveyed in one study described difficulty kissing, licking the lips or keeping the tongue clean, and embarrassment or teasing [2].

The consensus statement grouped ankyloglossia and sleep apnea as a category, with the authors stating that some statements did not reach consensus [13]. Wikipedia reports that some practitioners link a tied tongue to sleep-disordered breathing [2].

sections.h: Claims about posture, palate and facial structure
paras: Wikipedia describes proposed associations: restricted tongue contact with the palate may prolong an infantile swallow pattern and could contribute to an open bite; forceful tongue thrusting may contribute to a prominent lower jaw; ankyloglossia is correlated with a narrow, V-shaped palate, tooth crowding, bruxism, jaw-joint pain and mouth breathing; and a hypothesised fascial link may spread tension to the neck and jaw, described as speculative [2]. Whether release changes facial symmetry has not been established [2].

In looksmaxxing, tongue-tie release is connected to mewing, the tongue-posture practice associated with the British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, which proponents say reshapes the jaws by pressing the tongue to the roof of the mouth. Wikipedia reports that no credible scientific research has proven orthotropics, that the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw, and that Mike Mew was struck off the UK dental register in 2024; it does not discuss tongue-tie in that article [21]. The looksmax.org thread on adult release shows how the two ideas are combined by users [22].

For the upper lip, a systematic review of 11 studies found two frenum subtypes associated with a gap between the upper front teeth (maxillary midline diastema), and advised that superior labial frenectomy wait until permanent lateral incisors erupt, with orthodontic treatment first; a 1977 study of the diastema, the frenum and frenectomy is an early reference on that question [14][25].

On looksmax.org, an adult user describes an underdeveloped jaw that he attributes to poor tongue posture from a tongue-tie and asks whether release in his mid-twenties would improve his profile or is too late after puberty; a reply says it is worth doing because the tongue may relapse if it cannot be held up [22]. Proponents in such threads treat release as a step that makes tongue posture practices possible, while clinical sources describe the evidence base as concerned with feeding, speech and mobility [12][22].

The Cochrane review reported no serious complications in the trials reviewed, but said the small number of infants limited confidence [9]. The 2017 JAMA review characterised frenotomy as a low-risk procedure [12], and the FROSTTIE trial recorded three infants with adverse events after surgery [16]. Frenotomy is performed by pediatricians, otolaryngologists, dentists, oral surgeons and others; the 2020 consensus statement addressed informed consent [13]. Coverage varies; Wikipedia says public healthcare such as the NHS may not cover the procedure [20].

No studies found testing tongue-tie release for facial symmetry or appearance. Studies of frenotomy for infant feeding, speech and surgical technique exist [3][4][5][9][10][11], and trials of frenectomy techniques are registered, including adults with a high frenum attachment (NCT06331325, n=46) and tongue mobility after frenectomy (NCT06856564, n=60) [7][8].

timeline.event: A clinical study examines the diastema, the frenum and frenectomy [25].
Hazelbaker publishes an assessment tool for lingual frenulum function [2].
Messner and colleagues report breastfeeding difficulties in more mothers of infants with ankyloglossia than controls [2].
A comparison of CO2 laser and scalpel frenectomy assesses patient perceptions [5].
A review of facts and myths in diagnosis and treatment of ankyloglossia is published [3].
A randomised trial of early frenotomy in 107 breastfed infants is published [18].
The Cochrane review of frenotomy in newborns, a JAMA Otolaryngology review and a prospective cohort of tongue-tie and lip-tie release are published [9][12][4].
The AAO-HNS Delphi consensus statement on ankyloglossia in children is published, and professionals raise concern about unnecessary infant frenectomies [13][20].
A randomised trial of frenotomy for posterior tongue-tie and a systematic review of the upper lip frenum and diastema are published [17][14].
The UK FROSTTIE trial reports; it stopped early with 169 infants randomised [16].
Meta-analyses of breastfeeding and speech outcomes after frenotomy are published [10][11].
A double-blind sham-controlled newborn trial from Tampa General Hospital is published [15].

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums, tongue-tie release is discussed mainly as a way to enable better tongue posture and, through that, palate and jaw development, in the context of mewing and tongue posture discussions [22]. Clinical literature addresses release for infant feeding, speech and mobility instead [12].

claims.claim: A tongue-tie causes poor tongue posture that underdevelops the jaw.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster attributes his underdeveloped jaw to poor tongue posture from a tongue-tie [22].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes links between tongue-tie, palate shape and jaw features as proposed associations and not established outcomes [2].

claims.claim: Releasing a tongue-tie in adulthood can improve the side profile.
claims.believers: Users ask whether release in their mid-twenties helps, and one reply says it is worth doing to avoid relapse [22].
claims.experts: No study found tests release for facial symmetry or appearance.

claims.believers: Parents and practitioners report improved latch and less pain after release [4][17].
claims.experts: The Cochrane review found reduced nipple pain but not consistent improvement in infant feeding [9]; a 2024 meta-analysis reported improved self-efficacy and pain [10]; a sham-controlled trial found no immediate difference [15].

claims.claim: Posterior tongue-tie is a real cause of feeding problems.
claims.believers: A 2022 trial of 47 infants reported objective feeding improvement after frenotomy [17].
claims.experts: The 2017 JAMA review described confusion over which infants need treatment and a lack of high-quality studies [12]; consensus statements left some questions without agreement [13].

claims.believers: Parents and speech therapists report articulation improvements after frenectomy [19].
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis associated frenectomy with improved articulation in selected children [11], while Wikipedia reports later reviews finding no effect of ankyloglossia on speech sound development [2].

claims.claim: A tied tongue affects sleep and breathing.
claims.believers: Some practitioners link tongue-tie to sleep-disordered breathing, and a cohort reported improved sleep after frenectomy [2][19].
claims.experts: The consensus panel included ankyloglossia and sleep apnea among topics, with some statements not reaching consensus [13].

claims.claim: The lip frenum causes a gap between the front teeth that release prevents.
claims.believers: Parents are influenced by online advice about aesthetics [14].
claims.experts: A systematic review found no consensus on whether superior labial frenectomy prevents diastema and advised waiting for permanent incisors [14].

claims.believers: Parents in online groups seek release for feeding difficulties [20].
claims.experts: Professionals raised concerns in 2020 about unnecessary frenectomies partly driven by online groups [20], and a 10-fold increase in upper lip frenectomies since 2000 has been reported [14].
